analysis.one_liner: Cuts and caps federal spending and ties any debt limit increase to a balanced budget amendment.
analysis.headline: Introduced in August 2012 with 22 Republican cosponsors, the bill was referred to the Senate Budget Committee and never received a hearing, a vote, or floor action before the Congress ended in January 2013.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would cut fiscal 2013 spending, set ten-year limits on defense and nondefense spending, and let automatic across-the-board cuts fall on programs that exceed their caps, including uniform reductions to every Social Security benefit and to all Medicare outlays. It would bar the Treasury from using additional borrowing authority until Congress sends the states a balanced budget amendment that also requires supermajority votes for any tax increase. Defense budgets would rise every year while domestic discretionary spending would be frozen near the same dollar level for a decade.
analysis.who_benefits: Defense budgets and contractors, whose spending limits rise from $546 billion to $654 billion over ten years while nondefense spending is frozen flat; higher-income households, shielded by a required constitutional amendment that makes tax increases far harder to pass and targets revenue at 18% of GDP; and holders of Treasury debt, who would get a debt limit increase to $17.4 trillion, though only after the amendment is sent to the states.

how_it_helps.text: Raises the public debt limit to $17.4 trillion, preventing a default on Treasury obligations, but only once a balanced budget amendment is transmitted to the states for ratification.
Sets defense discretionary limits that grow each year for a decade, from $546 billion to $654 billion in budget authority.

States it is the sense of Congress that tax reform should hold revenue to the historical average of 18% of GDP while lowering marginal rates, and the required constitutional amendment would need a supermajority vote in both chambers for any tax increase.

analysis.who_pays: If spending exceeds the caps, every Social Security benefit and all Medicare outlays would be cut by a uniform percentage with no flexibility, veterans' benefits would be cut to fit their cap, and nondefense domestic programs would be frozen at roughly $440 billion a year for ten years, which after inflation means a real cut to education, transportation, medical research, and other domestic services.
analysis.who_pays_short: Seniors, veterans, and domestic program users

drawbacks.text: If the Social Security or Medicare caps are breached, the law would require the programs themselves to cut every benefit and every outlay by the same uniform percentage, with no protection for low-income or disabled beneficiaries.
Nondefense discretionary spending would be held near $439-449 billion for fiscal 2013 through 2022, a nominal freeze that is a real cut once inflation is counted, while defense caps climb every year.

The Treasury would be prohibited from exercising additional borrowing authority until a balanced budget amendment requiring supermajority approval of tax increases is transmitted to the states, a condition that could take years or never be met and risks default on federal obligations.
Supporters' goal of deficit reduction is legitimate, but the design is blunt: automatic proportional benefit cuts and a decade-long domestic freeze leave no room to choose which programs matter most.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: Deficit reduction and a raised debt limit are real goals, but the bill achieves them by freezing domestic spending for a decade while letting defense budgets grow, and by making Social Security and Medicare benefit cuts automatic and uniform if caps are breached. The demand that the debt limit be held hostage to a constitutional amendment requiring supermajority tax votes made the bill impossible to pass and put default risk ahead of any actual deficit reduction.

outcome.mechanism: It sat in the Senate Budget Committee from its introduction in August 2012 until the Congress ended in January 2013, never receiving a hearing, a vote, or floor time.

narrative.text: Senator Mike Lee introduced the bill on August 2, 2012, and it was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on the Budget.
Twenty-two Republican senators joined as cosponsors; no Democrat did.
The bill took no further action for the rest of the 112th Congress, which ended January 3, 2013.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Seniors and veterans were better off because a bill that would have cut every Social Security and Medicare benefit automatically if spending caps were breached never advanced. Bondholders were also better off that a debt limit increase conditioned on ratification of a constitutional amendment never became the operative law.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Seniors and veterans spared automatic benefit cuts

for.name: Sen. Mike Lee
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Cut, Cap, and Balance Act of 2012 in the Senate.

against.name: Sen. Harry Reid
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to the Senate floor.

against.name: Sen. Kent Conrad
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a committee markup or vote on the bill after it was referred.

sides.party_line_note: All 23 sponsors and cosponsors were Republicans, and the Democratic majority that controlled the Senate took no action on the bill.

industries.note: The bill's discretionary caps let defense budget authority grow every year for a decade, from $546 billion to $654 billion, while nondefense spending is frozen flat, so the defense share of a shrinking budget rises. That prioritization comes at the cost of domestic programs ordinary people use.

If Medicare outlays exceed the cap, the bill requires uniform percentage cuts to all outlays, reducing provider payments and beneficiary access at the same time. Providers and patients would lose together.

The bill locks in a revenue target of 18% of GDP with lower marginal rates and requires a constitutional amendment under which tax increases need supermajority votes in both chambers, making tax increases on high earners structurally much harder. The cost of deficit reduction is shifted onto program cuts instead.
The bill raises the debt limit to $17.4 trillion, which would prevent default on government debt, though only after a balanced budget amendment is transmitted to the states.
